thesis.title:
Distributed subsidy management

on Hyperledger Fabric
thesis.body: The application layer of a research prototype for EU agricultural subsidies in Greece, run by seven organisations on a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric network. Go chaincodes and services, React/TypeScript portals, farmers who hold their own keys and sign in the browser, and private data shared only with the organisations that need it.

thesisPage.title: Designing Trust Across Seven Organisations
thesisPage.subtitle: A permissioned dApp for verifiable agricultural subsidy workflows
thesisPage.description: B.Sc. thesis case study: a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric application for multi-organisation subsidy workflows, where farmers sign in their own browser wallet.
thesisPage.department: Informatics and Telematics, Harokopio University of Athens

signing.title: The farmer signs, not the platform

testing.title: Engineering for the failure that still looks successful

overview.question: Most public-service software digitises a form. This project asked a harder question:
overview.statement: Can the decision behind a subsidy become independently verifiable, without giving one organisation complete control of the workflow or custody of the citizen’s signing key?
overview.p1: For my B.Sc. thesis I designed and built the application layer of a research platform for agricultural subsidies on Hyperledger Fabric. Seven participants share one workflow. Policy rules run as deterministic smart contracts, sensitive records reach only the organisations that need them, and farmers sign their own transactions from a browser wallet.
overview.disclaimer: It is a fully implemented research prototype. It is not an official OPEKEPE service, not an official implementation of the EU Common Agricultural Policy and not a production government service: the institutional registries are simulated, and no real funds move.
overview.attribution: The thesis was written in two parts. I built the application layer described on this page; <anastasia>Anastasia Zerva</anastasia> led the Hyperledger Fabric infrastructure, its orchestration and the network evaluation.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.roleValue: Application architect, blockchain and full-stack engineer, wallet developer, researcher
glance.scopeValue: Chaincodes and smart contracts, application services, external-system connectors, seven role-specific portals, the farmer wallet, end-to-end workflows and application-level testing
glance.collaborationValue: Two-part thesis with Anastasia Zerva, who led the Fabric infrastructure, orchestration and network evaluation

challenge.lead: Agricultural subsidy administration is not one transaction between a citizen and an application. It is a long-running process across several authorities, with private records, changing policy rules, eligibility checks, approvals and payment instructions.

history.title: Nobody rewrites history alone
history.body: No single organisation should be able to silently rewrite the history of a case. The parties need a shared record, while their legal responsibilities stay distinct.

signing.title: The farmer authorises
signing.body: A farmer should authorise their own application. A server signing on their behalf is convenient, but it weakens non-repudiation and turns the service provider into a key custodian.

visibility.title: Verification without exposure
visibility.body: Shared verification must not mean shared visibility. Tax, land and banking records cannot reach every participant just because they work on the same process.

policy.title: Policy without a release
policy.body: Rates, thresholds, eligibility windows and penalty scales change. Hard-coding them would tie every regulatory change to a new deployment.

challenge.goal: The goal was not to put the process on a blockchain. It was to decide precisely which facts belong on a shared ledger, which must stay private, who may move a case forward, and what evidence should remain after every decision.

design.principle: <line>Institutions keep control of their systems.</line> <line>The consortium shares only the proofs, decisions and state required to complete the process.</line>
design.p1: The platform separates three planes. The systems each institution already owns, such as its tax, land, reserve and banking registries, form the external plane. The connector plane is the only layer allowed to talk both to an institution’s registry and to its Fabric peer. The consortium plane holds the shared ledger and the smart contracts.
design.rule: Static architecture checks enforce the boundary: connectors cannot import a database driver, and external registries cannot depend on Fabric.
design.p2: A consortium should integrate sovereign systems, not quietly absorb them into a new central database.

figure.caption: Three planes / one connector per organisation
figure.channel: Three chaincodes, five private data collections

architecture.p1: Seven organisations take part in one channel, subsidychannel. Six of them run their own infrastructure, and their staff sign in through Keycloak. Farmers run nothing: each holds an X.509 identity under FarmersMSP and signs in a browser wallet.
architecture.p2: Three chaincodes keep their world state in separate namespaces. Five private data collections narrow who can read sensitive values, and OPEKEPE is a member of every one of them.

figure.caption: System architecture / seven organisations on <name>subsidychannel</name>
figure.staffGroupNote: Staff sign in through Keycloak SSO

notes.observer: No consenter, cannot endorse or submit

figure.namespaceNote: Each chaincode keeps its world state and its private data collections in its own namespace.
figure.legendFarmer: Self-held key, signed in the browser

policy.p1: I split the on-chain domain into three chaincodes with separate responsibilities.

chaincodes.policy: Stores the active policy version, payment schemes, rates, thresholds and penalty parameters as ledger data.
chaincodes.entitlement: Manages the request, verification, allocation and issuance of subsidy entitlements.
chaincodes.subsidy: Manages the annual application, from submission and eligibility checks through approval and the payment order.

policy.testPolicy: The ledger runs a test policy, CAP-2026-v1, inspired by the Common Agricultural Policy and explicitly not legislation. A new policy period becomes a new version in the ledger, not a set of hidden constants in a code release.
policy.p2: Across the three chaincodes, fifteen contracts implement state transitions, access rules, deadlines, duplicate-claim prevention and subsidy calculations.
policy.guardsLabel: A transition goes through only when

guards.state: the current state of the case allows it
guards.caller: the caller’s MSP is authorised for it
guards.time: its deadline or time window holds
guards.duplicate: it does not duplicate an existing claim
guards.amount: every amount follows from a deterministic calculation

policy.timestamps: Timestamps come from the Fabric transaction context, never from a local clock, so every endorsing peer computes the same result.

signing.p1: The most distinctive part of the project is a Chrome-compatible wallet extension for citizen self-custody.
signing.p2: Each farmer has a real X.509 identity under a dedicated FarmersMSP. The wallet generates an ECDSA P-256 key pair in the browser, encrypts the private key at rest with AES-256-GCM under a PBKDF2-derived key, and offers an encrypted backup that the farmer controls. The private key is never sent to the portal or the backend.
signing.quote: <line>The backend may transport a transaction.</line> <line>The backend cannot authorise it on the farmer’s behalf.</line>
signing.p3: A browser cannot act as a native Fabric Gateway client, so I designed an offline-signing protocol. The wallet does not sign a byte array because a server sent it: it decodes the bytes and checks what they would authorise first.

flow.caption: Offline signing / two rounds, nine steps
flow.description: Nine steps in two rounds. Round 1, the proposal: the backend prepares an unsigned proposal, and the wallet decodes it, verifies it and signs it before the backend sends it for endorsement. Round 2, the transaction: the backend returns the transaction bytes, and the wallet verifies and signs the envelope before the backend submits it to ordering. The portal only relays bytes between wallet and backend.
flow.boundary: Trust boundary: the private key stays in the wallet

1.title: Prepare the proposal
1.detail: Unsigned, built from the farmer’s public identity

3.title: Check what it authorises
3.detail: Channel, chaincode function, MSP, certificate, farmer ID

5.title: Send for endorsement
5.detail: The signed proposal goes to the peers

6.title: Return the transaction
6.detail: Transaction bytes built from the endorsements

7.title: Verify the envelope
7.detail: Decoded and checked before a second signature

9.title: Submit to ordering
9.detail: Only now does the transaction reach the orderer

signing.readsIntro: The same identity protects reads. Each step closes a specific gap:

challenge.title: One-time challenge
challenge.body: A short-lived session starts from a single-use nonce.

message.title: Domain-separated signature
message.body: The wallet signs a message that cannot double as a signature on anything else.

chain.title: Certificate chain
chain.body: The backend validates it against the FarmersMSP CA.

identity.title: Farmer ID from the certificate
identity.body: Never from a query parameter, which closes an enumeration path against citizen records.

privacy.p1: One shared channel gives every participant the same process history, while five private data collections keep sensitive values with the organisations that need them. Tax and land data are shared only with the relevant authority and OPEKEPE. The bank resolves the IBAN inside its own registry; the IBAN never enters the ledger.
privacy.p2: Large or erasable documents take another path. A young farmer’s diploma is stored in a private two-node IPFS/Kubo swarm operated by separate organisations, and only its content identifier (CID) is committed to the workflow. That keeps an integrity reference without placing the PDF in immutable ledger state.
privacy.p3: A person still reviews the document: a hash proves that the content has not changed, not that it belongs to the applicant.
privacy.statement: <line>Immutability is useful for decisions and evidence.</line> <line>It is often the wrong property for personal documents.</line>

workflow.title: Workflow state and decisions
workflow.body: Every organisation’s peer keeps the same history of states and decisions. The EU Observer can read it, but cannot endorse or submit. Farmers have no peer and read their own case through signed requests.

records.title: Tax and land facts
records.body: Tax facts are shared only between OPEKEPE and AADE, land facts only between OPEKEPE and the Region. The other peers see a hash of each private value, which is how Fabric records private data on the shared ledger.

iban.title: Bank account (IBAN)
iban.body: OPEKEPE issues the payment order. The bank resolves the farmer’s IBAN in its own system, so the IBAN never enters the ledger.

diploma.title: Young farmer’s diploma
diploma.body: The PDF stays off the ledger, on two IPFS/Kubo nodes run by separate organisations. Only its CID is committed to the workflow, and a person still reviews the document.

perspectives.p1: The system includes seven role-specific React portals and a browser wallet. Each portal is a controlled window onto the same state machine, not a separate dashboard.
perspectives.p2: The backends react to chaincode events instead of relying on a central workflow engine. When a case reaches the relevant state, each organisation checks it against its own registry and records a signed result.

farmer.name: Farmers
farmer.body: Enrol, review entitlements, prepare applications and sign transactions.

opekepe.name: OPEKEPE
opekepe.body: Manages campaigns, registrations, escalations and final decisions.

ministry.name: Ministry
ministry.body: Decides on the National Reserve and co-approves high-value cases.

bank.name: Bank
bank.body: Processes payment orders without disclosing banking data to the consortium.

observer.name: EU Observer
observer.body: Receives an audit view of the ledger. It cannot endorse or submit state changes.

testing.statement: <line>In a payment system, the most dangerous defect is not always a crash.</line> <line>It is a workflow that completes normally with the wrong amount.</line>
testing.p1: That shaped the verification strategy. Tests assert exact monetary outcomes, authorised callers, legal state transitions, privacy boundaries and end-to-end ledger state, not only HTTP status codes.
testing.suites: Unit, integration, end-to-end, security and conformance suites. Private data isolation is checked live, from the peers of different organisations.

performance.p1: I benchmarked the self-custody signing path with a real proposal captured from the running system, timing decoding, verification, signing and DER encoding together.
performance.resultsLabel: Median time for the signing path
performance.p2: The cryptographic work was effectively imperceptible. Network endorsement and consensus, not client-side signing, dominated the wait. These are measurements on two machines, not a projection to other devices or loads.
performance.deployment: The platform also ran beyond a laptop: the consortium was deployed on six physical machines connected over WireGuard, with a cloud node serving the citizen-facing edge. That deployment belongs to Anastasia Zerva’s infrastructure half of the joint thesis; the application workflows described here ran on top of it.

simulated.title: Simulated registries, no real funds
simulated.body: The institutional registries are simulated, and the prototype cannot move real money.

policy.title: A test policy, not law
policy.body: <nb>CAP-2026-v1</nb> is representative. It is not an authoritative codification of EU law.

usability.title: Self-custody with real farmers is untested
usability.body: The signing flow was validated technically. Its usability with real farmers remains a future study.

erasure.title: Erasure is reduced, not solved
erasure.body: Keeping documents off-chain reduces the tension between an immutable ledger and the right to erasure, but some identifying fields still remain on-chain.

inputs.title: Contracts only know their inputs
inputs.body: A rule cannot be enforced if the domain model does not contain the fact it depends on. Smart-contract code cannot responsibly invent missing data.

limitations.closing: These constraints are not footnotes. They define where the system’s guarantees end.

learned.lead: The strongest result was not that a blockchain can record subsidy decisions. A conventional database can record them too.
learned.statement: The meaningful result was that authority can be distributed without making responsibility ambiguous.
learned.intro: The project became an exercise in a broader kind of engineering: designing not only what a system does, but who is allowed to know, decide, sign and prove each part of it.

know.title: Who may know
know.body: Tax and land facts reach only the relevant authority and OPEKEPE. Banking data stays at the bank.

decide.title: Who may decide
decide.body: OPEKEPE remains the payment authority, the tax agency answers for tax facts, and every transition checks the caller’s MSP.

sign.title: Who may sign
sign.body: The farmer holds the key that authorises the application. The platform carries the transaction but cannot sign it.

prove.title: What can be proven
prove.body: The ledger keeps a shared sequence of signed decisions that no participant can rewrite alone. A hash proves a document is unchanged, not whose it is.

outcome.p1: The thesis produced a working, measurable answer to its central question. A citizen can sign their own public-service transaction. Changing policy can be represented as governed, versioned data. Several institutions can coordinate on one ledger without exposing every underlying record. And verification can focus on whether decisions are correct, not only on whether the software is available.

ergohubPage.metaTitle: ErgoHub: From Application Code to a Kubernetes Cluster
ergohubPage.title: From Application Code to a Kubernetes Cluster
ergohubPage.subtitle: ErgoHub, a freelance marketplace: a Spring Boot and React application, and the Docker, Jenkins and Ansible path that deployed it to Azure Kubernetes Service
ergohubPage.description: ErgoHub, a team academic project: a Spring Boot and React freelance marketplace, deployed to Azure Kubernetes Service with Docker, Jenkins and Ansible.
ergohubPage.team: Team of two, with Anastasia Zerva
ergohubPage.context: Harokopio University of Athens: Distributed Systems, then DevOps Concepts & Tools

pipeline.title: Six pipeline definitions, three ways to deploy

challenges.title: What broke when the pieces met

overview.statement: Building the application was only half the problem. The other half was the path from a commit to a running cluster, and making that path repeatable.
overview.p1: ErgoHub is a freelance marketplace with three roles. Clients post projects, and an administrator approves or denies each one before freelancers can see it. Freelancers apply, with a CV if they choose, and the client accepts one application, which starts the work.
overview.p2: It began as the project for the Distributed Systems course at Harokopio University of Athens. In DevOps Concepts & Tools we took it the rest of the way: container images, Jenkins pipelines, Ansible playbooks and a deployment on Azure Kubernetes Service.
overview.attribution: We were a team of two, <anastasia>Anastasia Zerva</anastasia> and I, and we both worked across the API, the front end and the delivery. So this page says “we”; the reflection at the end is mine.
overview.disclaimer: It was an academic project, deployed and presented for the course rather than run as a service, so there are no users, traffic or uptime figures to report.

paths.caption: Two paths through the project

application.label: Application
application.note: A request, from the browser to the data

user.name: User
user.body: Client, freelancer or administrator, in a browser

frontend.name: Front end
frontend.body: React and Redux Toolkit, served by NGINX

api.name: API
api.body: Spring Boot 3 on Java 21, with JWT and role checks

data.name: Data
data.body: PostgreSQL for records, MinIO for CV files

delivery.label: Delivery
delivery.note: A change, from the repository to the cluster

source.name: Source
source.body: One Git repository for the API and the front end

ci.name: CI
ci.body: Jenkins runs the tests and builds an image

registry.name: Registry
registry.body: Azure Container Registry, tagged with the build number

cluster.name: Kubernetes
cluster.body: AKS, rolled out with kubectl or Ansible

ingress.name: Ingress
ingress.body: NGINX Ingress, HTTPS with Let’s Encrypt

paths.meet: The two paths meet in the cluster: the front end and the API that answer each request are the images the delivery path built and rolled out.

application.lead: The API is a Spring Boot 3 application on Java 21. The front end is a React application with Redux Toolkit and a dashboard for each role, and it talks to the API over REST.

workflow.caption: A project, from posting to completion

steps.pending: A client posts a project. It waits for an administrator.
steps.approved: An administrator approves it or denies it. Freelancers see only approved projects.
steps.inProgress: Freelancers apply, with a CV if they choose. The client accepts one application; the others are rejected.
steps.completed: The freelancer or an administrator marks the work complete.

access.title: Access by role
access.body: Signing in returns a JSON Web Token, signed with a shared HMAC key and valid for 24 hours, which carries the user’s role and whether the account has been verified. The API keeps no session: Spring Security checks the token on each request and applies role rules per route. Passwords are stored as BCrypt hashes.

records.title: Records and files
records.body: Users, projects and applications live in PostgreSQL, through Spring Data JPA. A CV sent with an application goes to a MinIO bucket; the application keeps only its path, and the API serves the file back through a download endpoint.

mail.title: Mail
mail.body: Administrators verify freelancer accounts, and the API emails the freelancer when that happens. In the local Docker Compose setup, that mail went to MailHog, a test mail server.

tests.title: Tests
tests.body: The API has JUnit tests for its services, run against an in-memory H2 database. The front end has Jest tests with Testing Library. Both run in the pipelines before an image is built.

containers.lead: The API and the front end each have their own image, built in two stages: the first holds the build tools, the second only what runs.

api.title: API
api.body: The first stage installs Maven on a Java 21 image and packages the application. The second copies only the jar onto a fresh Java 21 slim image, listening on port 8080. The image build skips the tests, because the pipeline has already run them.

frontend.title: Front end
frontend.body: Node 21 builds the React application; NGINX on Alpine then serves the built files, with a configuration of its own.

containers.compose: Docker Compose ran the whole system on one machine: PostgreSQL 15, the API, the front end, MinIO, MailHog and Jenkins itself.
containers.tags: Both AKS paths push each image with two tags: the build number, which ties the image to the pipeline run that made it, and latest, which the Kubernetes manifests refer to.

pipeline.lead: The repository has six Jenkinsfiles: one for the API and one for the front end, for each of three ways to deploy.

kubectl.title: AKS with kubectl
kubectl.deployment: kubectl set image, then a wait for the rollout and a check on the pods

ansible.title: AKS with Ansible
ansible.deployment: An Ansible playbook applies the whole system in order, then checks it

minikube.title: Minikube with Ansible
minikube.deployment: An Ansible playbook deploys to a local Minikube cluster

stages.caption: Stages of the two kubectl pipelines, as named in their Jenkinsfiles

pipeline.p1: Both kubectl pipelines sign in to Azure with a service principal and to the registry with a token, push the image, point the Deployment at it with kubectl set image, and wait up to five minutes for the rollout before listing the pods. The front-end pipeline also runs ESLint and npm audit, which report problems without failing the build.
pipeline.p2: The Ansible pipelines hand the deployment to a playbook, which applies the system in order: the namespace, configuration and secrets; PostgreSQL, MailHog and MinIO, then a wait until they are ready; the API and the front end with the new image, and their Services; finally the Ingress, and checks on what is running.

kubernetes.lead: Everything ran in one namespace, freelance, from plain manifests applied with kubectl, whether by a setup script, a pipeline or Ansible. There is no Helm chart.

figure.caption: The <name>freelance</name> namespace on Azure Kubernetes Service
ingressNotes: TLS from Let’s Encrypt, through cert-manager
figure.hosts: Separate host names for the API, the MinIO console and MailHog
figure.configNote: A ConfigMap, freelance-config, and a Secret, read by the workloads as environment variables

kubernetes.p1: PostgreSQL and MinIO kept their data on persistent volume claims of 5 Gi and 10 Gi. Each ran as a single-replica Deployment rather than a StatefulSet: enough for a course deployment, not a design for failover.
kubernetes.p2: Every container had CPU and memory requests and limits. The API’s probes called /api/home, a path that needs no sign-in, so that Kubernetes could tell an application that was still starting from one that had failed.
kubernetes.p3: A setup script prepared the cluster once: it installed the NGINX ingress controller and cert-manager, created the Let’s Encrypt issuer and applied the manifests. After that, a run of a kubectl pipeline only had to roll out a new image.

challenges.lead: The last week of June 2025 went less into features than into problems that only appear once the pieces run together. Four of them, from the commit history:

reach.title: Jenkins could not reach the cluster
reach.body: Jenkins ran in a container, and the local Minikube cluster was outside it. The address in its kubeconfig went through host.docker.internal, the Minikube IP, a kubectl proxy and the Docker bridge gateway. The AKS pipelines settled it differently: they fetch a kubeconfig from Azure at the start of each run.

probes.title: Health checks against a secured API
probes.body: Every path behind Spring Security needs a token, and a Kubernetes probe has none. We pointed the probes at /api/home, a path that needs no sign-in, and added a startup probe with longer delays, so that a slow start was not taken for a failure.

memory.title: The API ran out of memory
memory.body: The API container was killed for going over its memory. We raised its memory and gave the JVM an explicit heap limit through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, so that it stayed inside the container’s limit.

names.title: Names and tags that had to match
names.body: The ConfigMap named services that did not match the Services in the manifests, and the Ansible pipelines had to be told which tag to deploy: the build number of the image just pushed, or latest for the part that had not changed.

learned.lead: The project moved where I think an application ends. It does not end when the tests pass; it ends when something outside the program can start it, check it and reach it.

health.title: Health is an interface
health.body: Kubernetes knows an application only through its probes. The path they call is part of the API like any other, with access rules of its own, and if it is wrong, a working service gets restarted.

config.title: Configuration crosses boundaries
config.body: A service name in a ConfigMap, an image tag passed to a playbook: what broke were values written in one file and read in another. They need the same care as code, and one place where they are defined.

limits.title: Limits belong to the program
limits.body: A memory limit on a container is half a setting. The program inside has its own view of how much memory it may use, and the two have to be chosen together.

written.title: Written down, not remembered
written.body: By the end, signing in to the registry, rolling out an image and waiting for it were steps in a pipeline or a playbook, not commands someone had to remember. That is what made the second deployment the same as the first.

openstackPage.metaTitle: OpenStack: A Private Cloud Inside One Google Cloud VM
openstackPage.title: A Private Cloud Inside One Google Cloud VM
openstackPage.subtitle: OpenStack on a single Google Cloud VM, and the Linux networking that let its instances reach the outside and survive a restart
openstackPage.description: Individual academic project: OpenStack deployed with DevStack on a Google Cloud VM, and the Linux networking and debugging that made its instances reachable.
openstackPage.platform: DevStack on Ubuntu 24.04, Google Cloud n2-standard-4
openstackPage.context: Harokopio University of Athens: Cloud Computing Management

environment.title: One VM, two layers of virtualisation

openstack.title: One tenant, as an administrator would hand it over

network.title: Two networks that did not know about each other

debugging.title: Following a packet to where it disappeared

application.title: An API and its database on the tenant network

environment.p1: The assignment was to run OpenStack and administer one tenant end to end: its project and user, quotas, network and instances, and an application on them. I ran DevStack on a single Google Cloud VM.
environment.p2: That puts two hypervisors in one stack. The VM is the first layer; the instances Nova starts are virtual machines inside it. I created it with nested virtualisation enabled.

openstack.lead: DevStack installed OpenStack on that one host, its services running as 24 systemd units. Inside it I built a single tenant:

services.keystone: a project, a user with the member role and an openrc file for that user
services.glance: an Ubuntu 22.04 Minimal image for both instances
services.neutron: a private network and subnet, a router to the public network, a security group and floating IPs

openstack.scope: Keeping the tenant apart from admin caused the most trouble. Of the 18 problems I logged, 8 came from creating or looking up a resource with the admin credentials: a security group “not found”, an “invalid” key pair, an instance with no private address. A resource belongs to the project that created it, so the credentials in use decide what exists.

network.p1: An instance’s traffic crosses two networks. Inside OpenStack, the Neutron router gives it an address from the floating range and sends it out through br-ex, the host’s Open vSwitch bridge for the external network. Outside, Google Cloud knows one address for the whole machine: the VM’s internal address on ens4, its only network interface.
network.p2: Nothing joined the two: the lab instructions, written for VirtualBox, did not cover it, so the host had to route and translate the traffic itself.
network.p3: Bridging ens4 into br-ex was not an option. I had run that one ovs-vsctl command in an early lab: it took the VM’s only interface out of the host’s network stack, SSH dropped, the serial console could not recover it, and I rebuilt the VM from scratch. From then on, ens4 stayed the host’s, and traffic was routed to it, not bridged.

figure.caption: The layers an instance’s traffic crosses, inside one Google Cloud VM
figure.googleNote: Forwards traffic from the VM only when its source is the VM’s own address
figure.iptables: MASQUERADE on ens4, FORWARD between br-ex and ens4, saved with iptables-persistent
figure.brex: Open vSwitch bridge for OpenStack’s external network
figure.brexSetup: A oneshot unit that restores the bridge’s address and the floating-range route at boot
figure.routerNote: Gateway on the public network, one floating IP per instance
figure.tenantNote: One security group: TCP 22, 80 and 5432, and ICMP
figure.added: Added on the host to connect the layers
figure.testPath: SSH tunnel through the host to vm-app, port 80

symptom.label: Symptom
symptom.body: In the first instance, ping got no reply and apt update hung at “Connecting to archive.ubuntu.com”. No error, anywhere.

trace.label: Trace
trace.body: tcpdump on each interface along the path: the packets showed up on the instance’s tap interface and on br-ex, never on ens4.

cause.label: Cause
cause.body: The host was not forwarding between br-ex and ens4, and anything it did forward would leave with a floating-range source address, which Google Cloud drops without a reply.

fix.label: Fix
fix.body: IP forwarding on; FORWARD rules out from br-ex and back for established connections only; MASQUERADE on ens4; all saved with iptables-persistent.

debugging.persistence: That held until the VM was stopped and started again. The iptables rules came back, but br-ex came up without its address and route, and the floating IPs were unreachable again. I kept a checklist of commands to rerun, then replaced it with brex-setup.service, a oneshot systemd unit ordered after the network and DevStack that restores the bridge at boot.
debugging.lesson: The lessons I kept: the fault lies one step past the last interface where the packet is still visible, and a fix that a restart undoes is not finished until it is part of the boot.

application.p1: To test the tenant end to end, I deployed a small two-tier application. The lab exercises put PostgreSQL and Flask on one VM; I split them across two instances, so that the API had to reach its database over OpenStack’s private network.
application.p2: vm-db runs PostgreSQL 14, set to accept remote connections. vm-app runs a Flask API under Gunicorn as a systemd service, behind NGINX on port 80, and reaches vm-db by its private address. The final check went through an SSH tunnel via the host: /api/products returned four products as JSON, read from the other instance.

reflection.body: It worked, and it was built for a lab. Both instances share one security group, so PostgreSQL’s port is open on the application VM and port 80 on the database; I would give each tier its own group, with 5432 open only to vm-app. The database password sits in the application code, and PostgreSQL listens on every interface. And the host’s networking belongs in how the VM is provisioned, not in fixes added along the way.

cudaPage.metaTitle: CUDA: Matrix Multiplication from 306 ms to 86 ms
cudaPage.title: From 306 ms to 86 ms
cudaPage.subtitle: A CUDA matrix multiplication on an NVIDIA T4, rewritten twice to reuse data from faster memory, and measured after each step
cudaPage.description: Individual academic project: matrix multiplication in CUDA on an NVIDIA T4, from a naive kernel to shared-memory tiling and register blocking, timed per step.
cudaPage.platform: NVIDIA Tesla T4 (16 GB) on Google Colab, CUDA C
cudaPage.context: Harokopio University of Athens: Modern Parallel Architectures and High-Performance Programming

baseline.title: One thread per element, every operand from global memory

bottleneck.title: Two loads from global memory for every multiply-add

optimisation.title: Reuse in shared memory, then in registers

result.title: A 3.6× speedup, for these kernels on this GPU

baseline.lead: I implemented C = A × B for square N × N single-precision matrices in CUDA C and timed it from N = 128 to 4096. At N = 4096, each of the 16.8 million elements of C is a sum of 4096 products.
baseline.p2: The first kernel is the direct translation: one thread per element of C, in blocks of 16 × 16 threads. Each thread walks its row of A and its column of B in global memory, the GPU’s main memory.

timer.label: Timer
timer.body: gettimeofday around one launch and cudaDeviceSynchronize, so copies from host to GPU are excluded

inputs.label: Inputs
inputs.body: the same seeded random matrices for every kernel; C set to zero before each

runs.label: Runs
runs.body: one Colab session, one timed launch per kernel and size

check.label: Check
check.body: the sum of all elements of C, in double precision

baseline.warmup: The session’s first launch, the naive kernel at N = 128, took 0.159 s, about 300 times its time at N = 256, and nothing like it happened again. I counted it as start-up cost and left N = 128 out of the comparisons.

bottleneck.lead: I did not profile the kernels, so this step is reasoning from the code. The naive kernel loads two values from global memory for every multiply-add: 8,192 loads for each element of C at N = 4096.
bottleneck.p2: Most of those loads repeat. The 16 threads in a row of a block read the same row of A, the 16 in a column the same column of B, and each fetches its own copy. What had to change was not the arithmetic but where its operands came from.

optimisation.lead: Two changes, each measured before the next.
optimisation.tiling: The 256 threads of a block copy a 16 × 16 tile of A and one of B into shared memory, the fast on-chip memory they share, then wait at a barrier. Each thread does 16 multiply-adds from the tiles before the next pair is loaded. Every value fetched now serves 16 threads: 512 global loads per element of C instead of 8,192.
optimisation.registers: Each thread computes a 4 × 4 block of C and keeps its 16 running sums in registers, the fastest storage on the GPU. At each step it reads four values of A and four of B from shared memory and multiplies every pair: 16 multiply-adds for 8 reads, where the tiled kernel did 1 for 2.
optimisation.caveat: That kernel also doubled the tiles to 32 × 32 and cut blocks to 64 threads, which halves the global loads again, to 256 per element. The 2.2× belongs to that combination, not to register blocking alone. And 16 times fewer global loads bought 1.6×, not 16×: they were not the whole cost, and without a profiler I cannot say what the rest was.

figure.caption: Kernel time at N = 4096 on an NVIDIA T4
figure.note: One timed launch per kernel, copies from host to GPU excluded. A shorter bar is faster.

result.p1: That ratio holds for this size on this T4: across N = 256 to 4096, the speedup of the third kernel over the first ranged from 3.2× to 5.8×.
result.correctness: All three kernels returned the same checksum at every size. That shows they agree with each other; it is not an element-by-element check against a reference result.
result.lesson: The lesson: work out where every operand comes from before changing code, and measure after each change. Next time I would change one thing at a time, so register blocking gets a number of its own, repeat every timing after a warm-up, and profile, so the reasoning about memory becomes a measurement.

visionPage.metaTitle: Computer Vision: Classification, Segmentation and Detection in PyTorch
visionPage.title: Classification, segmentation and detection in PyTorch
visionPage.subtitle: Five exercises with networks trained from scratch or fine-tuned from pretrained weights, ending in a Vision Transformer compared with a CNN
visionPage.description: Individual academic project: five computer vision exercises in PyTorch, from ResNet18 classification and a ViT/VGG comparison to U-Net and Faster R-CNN.
visionPage.platform: PyTorch and torchvision on Google Colab GPUs
visionPage.context: Harokopio University of Athens: Computer Vision and Graphics

classification.title: From a small CNN to a fine-tuned ResNet18

segmentation-detection.title: A U-Net from scratch and a detector fine-tuned from COCO

lessons.title: What these numbers can and cannot show

classification.lead: A CNN with three convolutional layers, trained from scratch on <nb>CIFAR-100</nb>, reached 30.62% to 42.13% test accuracy across three optimiser settings, while its training accuracy rose to about 80% in the two stronger runs.
classification.p2: I then adapted ResNet18, pretrained on ImageNet, to the 37 breeds of <nb>Oxford-IIIT</nb> Pet, in three runs of ten epochs:

runs.featureExtraction: backbone frozen; only a new 37-class output layer trained
runs.fineTuning: every layer trained at a learning rate of 0.0001, continuing from the run above
runs.augmentation: random rotations and horizontal flips, fine-tuned again from the ImageNet weights

classification.p3: Fine-tuning gave the best result, with training accuracy at 100%. Augmentation did not raise test accuracy, but that run restarted from the ImageNet weights, so the comparison is not clean.

comparison.lead: The last exercise compared a Vision Transformer, <nb>ViT-B/16</nb>, with a CNN, <nb>VGG16-BN</nb>, on <nb>CIFAR-10</nb>. Both started from ImageNet weights with a new 10-class output layer, and I trained all parameters of each the same way: 224 × 224 inputs, no augmentation, Adam at 0.0001, batches of 64.

table.caption: CIFAR-10 test accuracy at the last epoch
table.note: One run per model and length, without a fixed seed, on an NVIDIA A100. Time per epoch includes testing on 10,000 images.

comparison.p1: <nb>ViT-B/16</nb> finished {low} to {high} percentage points ahead, at about {ratio} times the time per epoch. Over ten epochs, the test loss of <nb>VGG16-BN</nb> rose from 0.216 after the second epoch to 0.270, while that of <nb>ViT-B/16</nb> stayed below 0.20. That holds for this dataset and setup; it does not rank the two architectures.

segmentation-detection.segmentation: I built a U-Net from scratch and trained it for 15 epochs on SBD, at 256 × 256 pixels in 21 classes, holding out a fifth of the 8,498 training images for evaluation.
segmentation-detection.detection: I fine-tuned torchvision’s <nb>Faster R-CNN</nb>, with a <nb>ResNet-50</nb> FPN backbone and COCO weights, on the 2,501 images of the VOC 2007 train split, with a new predictor for its 20 classes plus background.
segmentation-detection.p1: Of three optimiser setups, AdamW reached the lowest training loss, 0.144. But training loss is not detection quality: I computed no mAP and only checked predictions by eye. Likewise, pixel accuracy includes the background, and without IoU it does not show how well each class was segmented.

lessons.lead: What I took from these exercises: write the metric and the split beside every number, and compare models only under one setup.
lessons.p1: Two things I would change. In the classification exercises the test split doubled as the validation set checked after each epoch, so I report the last epoch, not the best; a separate validation split would fix that. And the comparison had one run per model without a fixed seed: after five epochs, two runs of the same <nb>VGG16-BN</nb> setup stood at 92.84% and 93.35%. Several seeds, plus IoU and mAP, would make these comparisons firmer.

energyPage.metaTitle: Energy Data Mining: Classifying and Forecasting Household Consumption
energyPage.title: Classifying and forecasting household energy use
energyPage.subtitle: A public UCI dataset of one household’s minute readings over almost four years, aggregated to 1,418 days and used for two tasks: labelling high-consumption days and forecasting the next day’s total
energyPage.description: Team academic project: high-consumption days classified with Gradient Boosting (89.4% test accuracy), next-day consumption forecast with Random Forest and LSTM.
energyPage.context: Harokopio University of Athens: Data Mining

classification.lead: A day counts as high when its total reaches {threshold} kWh, the mean of the training days alone. We split the {days} days in time order, 60/20/20, so the {test} test days come last.
classification.p2: The ten features describe the same day: sub-meter totals, peak-hour power, night-time energy, mean voltage and the calendar. So the model labels a day after the fact; it does not predict one. We removed mean current, which nearly restates the total, since power is voltage times current.
classification.p3: Random Forest ({rf}) and logistic regression ({lr}) reached slightly lower test accuracy. Only {high} of test days are high, so answering “not high” every time would already score {majority}; that is why F1 and <nb>ROC-AUC</nb> sit beside accuracy.

forecasting.lead: Here the target is the next day’s total in kWh, and the reference is persistence: tomorrow equals today. Each model was tuned or checked on the validation days, refitted on training plus validation and scored once on the test period.
forecasting.p1: We took two routes. A Random Forest regressor used twelve features of the current day; Ridge regression, its linear counterpart, had a test RMSE of <nb>{ridge} kWh</nb>. An LSTM used only the last 14 days of consumption.

figure.caption: Next-day forecast: test RMSE, lower is better

models.randomForest: twelve features of the current day

figure.note: Bars start at zero; the baseline is the full width. The two models come from separate setups, scored over almost the same test period ({features} and {history} days); persistence scores {baseline} in both.

forecasting.p2: Random Forest’s test RMSE was <nb>{gap} kWh</nb> below that of the LSTM run in our report. The LSTM was not seeded, though, and the last saved run of the notebook gave <nb>{lastRun} kWh</nb>, so in this experiment we read the two as level.

comparison.lead: The test RMSE of Ridge regression, Random Forest and the LSTM fell between {low} and <nb>{high} kWh</nb>, against <nb>{baseline} kWh</nb> for persistence. Without that baseline, the errors alone would say little.
comparison.p1: The two tasks also needed different measures: when one class is more common, accuracy alone flatters a classifier, and a forecast error means something only beside a naive reference. One comparison we would redo: <nb>ARIMA(1,1,1)</nb> and Prophet were scored on a single forecast of the whole test period, made before its first day rather than one day at a time, so their errors are not comparable and are left out.

about.label: About
about.statement: I like understanding how the pieces of a system fit together.
about.p1: I recently completed a B.Sc. in Informatics and Telematics at Harokopio University of Athens. Over the degree, my work moved steadily toward the server side and the infrastructure underneath it.
about.p2: What interests me most is how components communicate, where data and trust boundaries should live, and how software can be deployed, tested and operated reliably. My bachelor’s thesis gave me the opportunity to explore those questions across Go services, Hyperledger Fabric and browser-side cryptography.
about.p3: I’m now looking for graduate and junior engineering roles where I can keep building on that foundation in production systems.

curiosity.title: Curiosity
curiosity.p1: I was born and raised in Peristeri, Athens, and my first real encounter with technology wasn’t a programming language. It was a PlayStation 2. I loved the games, but even while playing, another question kept coming back: how is all of this actually built, and what is happening behind the screen?
curiosity.p2: At around twelve, an old desktop PC and an internet connection opened up a much larger world. I bought computer magazines, read the computer science books we had at school, spent hours on W3Schools and made my first attempts at building web pages. I experimented constantly with PCs and laptops too, changing things, breaking them, fixing them and learning by trying.
curiosity.p3: Somewhere in those years, computing stopped being something I was simply interested in and became a deliberate direction. I chose the informatics track at school and sat the national university entrance exams with one clear goal: to study computer science.

depth.title: Depth
depth.p1: University changed how I understood the field. The first two years were far more demanding than I had imagined, and that made computer science more compelling, not less. I enjoy difficult problems, particularly the point where something that first seems opaque begins to show its structure.
depth.p2: Two courses, DevOps and Computer Architecture, deepened that curiosity from opposite ends. DevOps showed me how source code becomes a system that is built, deployed, automated and operated. Computer Architecture went below the abstractions software relies on, closer to what the hardware itself is doing.
depth.pull: I want to understand before I implement.
depth.p3: I’m analytical and persistent, and I enjoy working as part of a team. When something doesn’t make sense to me yet, I find it hard to leave it unexamined. Knowing that something works is not enough: I want to know why it works, what it assumes, where its limits are and how it fits into the wider system.
depth.p4: Not everything I value from university shows up in a transcript. <anastasia>Anastasia Zerva</anastasia> and I have worked together since our first year, across assignments and projects. Over time, that grew into a long-term, research-oriented collaboration built on trust, complementary ways of thinking and a shared ambition to keep exploring difficult problems together.

direction.title: Direction
direction.p1: Today I don’t want to define myself by a single technology or one corner of computer science. My interests range widely, but the aim stays the same: to contribute through my work, to apply what I understand to real problems people face, and to build things that are useful in practice.
direction.p2: Outside computer science, I make time for friends and family, and I read regularly about economics, investing and entrepreneurship — other ways of thinking about systems, decisions and how value is created.
direction.callbackLead: In a way, I’m still asking the question I first had in front of that PlayStation 2:
direction.callback: What is happening underneath — and what can I build once I understand it?

ergohub.title:
Freelance marketplace

on Azure Kubernetes
ergohub.body: Clients post projects, an administrator approves or denies them, and freelancers apply, with a CV if they choose. We built the Spring Boot API and the React front end, then the path that delivers them: tested container images, a private registry, and a Kubernetes deployment on Azure behind NGINX Ingress and HTTPS.

openstack.name: OpenStack
openstack.title:
Private cloud deployment

on Google Cloud
openstack.body: OpenStack on one Google Cloud VM, deployed with DevStack and nested virtualisation. Most of the work was the network between the layers: floating IPs that existed only inside the host, packets Google Cloud dropped, a bridge that lost its routing on every restart. The result: a Flask API reading PostgreSQL over the tenant’s private network.

cuda.name: CUDA
cuda.title:
GPU matrix multiplication

with CUDA
cuda.body: Three CUDA kernels for <nb>4096 × 4096</nb> matrices on an <nb>NVIDIA T4</nb>. The first reads both operands of every multiply-add from global memory. The next two keep reused values in faster memory, through shared-memory tiling and then register blocking. All three give the same checksum.

vision.body: Five experiments in image classification, semantic segmentation and object detection, with models I trained from scratch or fine-tuned from ImageNet and COCO weights. The last compares a Vision Transformer with a CNN on <nb>CIFAR-10</nb> under one training setup, measuring test accuracy and time per epoch.

Each task has its own metrics, scored on test days held out until the end.
